Issues.Title: Design to keep Blazor's `/Error` page visible after WebAssembly activation
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Generate the Blazor Web App template's `/Error` page in the client project for global WebAssembly and global Auto interactivity. This lets both server endpoint routing and the interactive router resolve the same page. Keep the layout interactive and leave the app shell and router free of error-specific logic. No framework API or render-mode change is needed.

## Problem and root cause

The reported scenario is a fresh app created with `dotnet new blazor --all-interactive --interactivity WebAssembly`. On a direct visit to `/Error`, the server initially renders the Error page. Once WebAssembly activates, the interactive router replaces it with `NotFound`.

The template's generation rules move the router and layout to `.Client` for global WebAssembly and Auto, but leave the Error component in the server assembly. The server can see both assemblies, so it finds and prerenders `/Error`. The browser router matches the current URL using its client route table, which does not contain the server-only component.

The earlier #69998 was closed without merging. It moved the route to the client but also added error-specific request-ID plumbing to `App` and `Routes`. The [feedback](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69998#pullrequestreview-5840733412) was to keep specialized error handling out of those core template components.

## Proposed design

### Put `/Error` where both routers can find it

Update the template's [generation rules](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/.template.config/template.json) to generate Error under `.Client/Pages` when `UseWebAssembly && InteractiveAtRoot`. The server already registers the client assembly for Razor component endpoint discovery. Generate exactly one `/Error` component per app. Keep Error in the server project for static SSR, global Interactive Server, and per-page interactivity.

### Preserve the request ID without changing `App` or `Routes`

For the client-capable variant, register a server-only named cascading value at startup. The value supplies a callback that only the Error component invokes during prerendering. The callback preserves the current lookup order: server activity ID, then HTTP trace identifier. Apply the same registration to both generated server entry-point styles and only in the configurations that move Error.

The Error component persists only the resulting string through its existing `[PersistentState]` property. Neither `HttpContext` nor the callback crosses into WebAssembly. A later interactive visit with no corresponding server render must not display the previous request's ID. Check that behavior both when Auto selects Interactive Server and when it selects WebAssembly.

### Treat exception-handler re-execution as a separate path

A direct visit has `/Error` in the address bar. With `UseExceptionHandler("/Error")`, the server re-executes the request on `/Error`, but the browser URL remains the original path. Moving the component fixes the reported direct-route mismatch; it does not make the interactive router select `/Error` when the address bar contains a different route. Verify that real exception responses do not regress. If the original template already overwrites such an error response after activation, track that behavior separately.

## Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Why not choose it? |
|---|---|
| Mark `/Error` with `ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting` | Keeps Error visible but disables global interactivity for that request, including the layout. |
| Pass the request ID through `App` and `Routes` | Adds specialized error handling to core template components, as noted in the previous review. |
| Preserve server DOM on a route miss, add a router hook, or introduce a render mode | Changes framework behavior to solve a template route-placement bug. General SSR-to-client handoff is out of scope. |

## Acceptance criteria and validation

| Scenario | Expected result |
|---|---|
| Direct `/Error` with global WebAssembly | Error and its request ID are visible before and after WebAssembly activates; the layout responds to interaction. |
| Direct `/Error` with global Auto | Error and its request ID survive activation. Verify a visit on which Auto actually selects WebAssembly, not just an Interactive Server visit. |
| Navigate away, then return to `/Error` interactively | Error renders without reusing the original HTTP request ID. |
| Navigate to a genuinely missing route | Existing `NotFound` behavior is unchanged. |
| Generate static SSR, global Server, and per-page variants | `/Error` remains server-hosted. No configuration generates duplicate `/Error` endpoints. |
| Trigger a real server exception in Production | Confirm the HTTP 500 and Error response do not regress relative to the unmodified template. |

Verify the generated layout, including `--empty`, and exercise the handoff in the existing [Blazor template Playwright suite](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/src/ProjectTemplates/test/Templates.Blazor.Tests/BlazorWebTemplateTest.cs). The same post-activation assertion should fail on the unmodified template and pass with the fix. Checking the initial SSR HTML alone would miss the reported bug. Also verify the HTTP trace identifier fallback when no activity ID is available.

Issues.Title: Passkey login always fails with real authenticators: ES256 assertion signature verified as DER instead of raw r‖s
Issues.Body:
I registered a passkey through the new Identity passkey endpoints and registration worked fine — then every login failed with 401 "The assertion signature was invalid." After digging in, I found the server verifies ES256 assertion signatures in DER format, while real authenticators sign in raw r‖s format. The feature is effectively broken for real authenticators.

This is a functional bug, not a security issue: login fails closed, there is no bypass and no data leak. I'm filing it here rather than through MSRC for that reason.

### What I tested

I built a minimal Identity app with the passkey endpoints from main (commit `d0cdff50`, 25 Nov 2026) running on .NET 10.0.404, plus a Python harness that plays the authenticator. I ran the same 8 checks twice — same server, same keys, same scenarios — changing only the signature encoding:

- Raw r‖s (what real authenticators produce, 64 bytes for P-256): 6/8 passed. The two login checks failed with 401.
- DER: 8/8 passed, login returned 200 and the authenticated user came back correctly.

Registration, replay rejection, userHandle checks, and origin checks all behaved correctly in both runs — only login with a standard signature fails.

### Where it breaks

`src/Identity/Core/src/Passkeys/CredentialPublicKey.cs:111` verifies EC2 signatures with `DSASignatureFormat.Rfc3279DerSequence`. The only call site is `PasskeyHandler.cs:642` (assertion verification, step 21).

Per RFC 8152 §8.1, a COSE ECDSA signature is the raw concatenation `I2OSP(R, n) | I2OSP(S, n)` — that is what browsers, Windows Hello, iCloud Keychain, and security keys produce. DER is never what an authenticator sends.

This affects ES256, ES384, and ES512. RSA credentials are unaffected, and attestation isn't verified by the framework by default, so only the login path is hit.

### Why the tests missed it

Every test in the repo signs with DER too (`CredentialKeyPair.cs:86` and `MapIdentityApiTests.cs:2337` both use `Rfc3279DerSequence`), so the suite is consistent with the implementation and never exercises a raw signature from a real authenticator.

### Suggested fix

Verify with `DSASignatureFormat.IeeeP1363FixedFieldConcatenation` instead — or accept both encodings if there is a reason to keep DER working. Happy to open a PR if the maintainers agree on the approach.

### Environment

- ASP.NET Core main at `d0cdff50` (25 Nov 2026); endpoints as in .NET 10.0.404
- ES256 (P-256); also applies to ES384/ES512

Issues.Title: Bind inherited [AsParameters] properties in the Request Delegate Generator
Issues.Body:
Bind inherited `[AsParameters]` properties in the Request Delegate Generator

## Description

### Bug

With `EnableRequestDelegateGenerator` on, `[AsParameters]` binds only the properties that the parameter type declares itself. The generator never binds a property that a base class declares. That property keeps its default value. The runtime binder (`RequestDelegateFactory`) binds the same property. The generator reports no diagnostic.

For example, `GET /items?Page=2&PageSize=5&Name=x` returns `Page=2 PageSize=5 Name=x` with the runtime binder. It returns `Page=0 PageSize=0 Name=x` with the generator. The issue has the full repro.

A `required` property in a base class is worse: the generated object initializer does not set it, so the build fails with error CS9035.

### Cause

`TryGetAsParametersConstructor` in `EndpointParameter.cs` collects the properties with `type.GetMembers()`. This call returns only the members that the type declares. The runtime binder uses `Type.GetProperties()`. That call also returns the public properties of the base types.

### Fix

The new helper `GetPublicProperties` walks the type and its base types. It follows the rules of `Type.GetProperties()`:

- It includes the public properties that a base type declares.
- If a derived type overrides a property or hides it with `new`, the helper uses only the most derived declaration.
- A private property hides an inherited property only if the type itself declares it as an instance property. Reflection does the same.
- It does not return static properties of base types, as reflection does not. It does not return indexers.

The object initializer path also skips static properties. An object initializer cannot set a static property or an indexer, and `RequestDelegateFactory` fails on both with `InvalidProgramException`. Before, a public static property with a setter caused error CS1914 in the generated code, and a writable indexer caused invalid code. A constructor parameter can still match a static property that the type declares, as before.

Constructor matching, the emitted assignments, and the emitted parameter metadata all read this one list. Thus they all use the same set of properties.

Two more changes keep the generator in line with the runtime binder now that base types are in the list:

- The parameterless constructor path assigns a property only if it has a public setter. This is the same rule as `GetSetMethod(nonPublic: false) != null` in `RequestDelegateFactory`. A `required` property is also assigned, because the object initializer must set it. Before, a private or protected setter on a type from source caused error CS0272 in the generated code.
- The constructor lookup table is built only for a parameterized constructor, as in `ParameterBindingMethodCache.FindConstructor`. Before, two properties whose names differ only by case (for example `ID` in a base class and `Id` in the derived class) made the generator throw.

This change also fixes a related case. Before, a positional record that passes a parameter to a positional base record got the RDG006 warning, and the generator did not intercept the endpoint. Now the generator matches the constructor parameter to the inherited property.

### Behavior change

The public-setter rule also applies to properties that the `[AsParameters]` type declares itself. The generator used to assign these properties, and now it does not, as the runtime binder never did:

- A property with an `internal` setter, or with a `protected internal` setter in the same assembly.
- A getter-only override of a settable property.

A `required` property keeps its old behavior: the generator still assigns it.

### Tests

The new tests in `RequestDelegateCreationTests.AsParameters.cs` run two times: one time with the generator (`CompileTimeCreationTests`) and one time with the runtime binder (`RuntimeCreationTests`). They cover these cases:

- A property from a base class.
- A property from a grandparent class.
- A property that the derived class hides with `new`, and a property that the derived class overrides.
- Inherited properties with `[FromQuery(Name = ...)]` and `[FromHeader(Name = ...)]`.
- Inherited properties that are get-only, that have a private, protected, protected internal or private protected setter, or that a getter-only override replaces. The binder does not assign them.
- An inherited `required` property.
- An inherited property whose name differs only by case from a property of the derived class.
- A record constructor parameter that matches an inherited property.
- A constructor parameter that matches a static property. This worked before, and the test keeps it working.

The tests also check the `IParameterBindingMetadata` of the inherited and hidden properties.

A metadata reference hides private and internal members from the generator. Thus one more test in `CompileTimeCreationTests.AsParameters.cs` declares a hierarchy in source. It covers private and internal setters, a `required` property with an internal setter, a static property, a writable indexer, a private base property, a private static property, and a private instance property of the derived type.

No baseline file changes.

### Not changed

If a derived class hides a property with `new` and a different property type, both binders fail when the endpoint is built. The runtime binder adds the same parameter name two times. The generator emits a `typeof(T).GetProperty(name)` call that throws `AmbiguousMatchException`. That was true before this PR, and this PR does not change it.

### Backport

Please consider a backport of this fix to `release/10.0`, the current LTS release. Apps that turn the generator on get wrong values for inherited `[AsParameters]` properties, and nothing warns them. An inherited `required` property breaks the build. The fix is small, and the shared generator and runtime-binder tests cover it. The servicing risk is the behavior change above: the generator stops assigning a property with an `internal` setter, or a getter-only override, which the runtime binder also does not assign.

Fixes #70852

Issues.Title: Reset _requestBodyStarted in Http3Stream.Initialize
Issues.Body:
Http3Stream objects are pooled and reused across requests on the same QUIC connection, but Http3Stream.Initialize() did not reset _requestBodyStarted (Http2Stream resets its equivalent RequestBodyStarted). After a request with a DATA frame, later body-less requests on the same pooled stream were misclassified: ReceivedEmptyRequestBody returned false and IHttpRequestBodyDetectionFeature.CanHaveBody returned true.

This resets the field in Initialize() and adds a test that sends a request with a body followed by a body-less request on a reused stream and verifies CanHaveBody is false for the second one.

Fixes #70845

Issues.Title: Request Delegate Generator does not bind [AsParameters] properties declared in a base class
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

With `EnableRequestDelegateGenerator` on, `[AsParameters]` binds only the properties that the parameter type declares itself. Properties that a base class declares are never bound and keep their default values. The runtime binder (`RequestDelegateFactory`) binds them. The generator reports no diagnostic, so the endpoint silently ignores those query values.

The cause looks to be in `TryGetAsParametersConstructor`. It reads `type.GetMembers()`, which returns only the members declared on that type, not the inherited ones:
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/0ead77dee6634c2fd00960150b6bf75bf4cb7cc8/src/Http/Http.Extensions/gen/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.RequestDelegateGenerator/StaticRouteHandlerModel/EndpointParameter.cs#L480

### Expected Behavior

The generated binder binds the inherited properties, as the runtime binder does. If inherited properties are not supported, the generator reports a diagnostic and does not intercept the endpoint.

### Steps To Reproduce

`Repro.csproj`:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <PropertyGroup Condition="'$(UseRdg)' == 'true'">
    <EnableRequestDelegateGenerator>true</EnableRequestDelegateGenerator>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

`Program.cs`:

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();

app.MapGet("/items", GetItems);

app.Run();

static string GetItems([AsParameters] DerivedQuery query)
    => $"Page={query.Page} PageSize={query.PageSize} Name={query.Name}";

public class BaseQuery
{
    public int Page { get; set; }
    public int PageSize { get; set; }
}

public class DerivedQuery : BaseQuery
{
    public string? Name { get; set; }
}
```

1. Run with `dotnet run -p:UseRdg=false` and request `GET /items?Page=2&PageSize=5&Name=x`. The response is `Page=2 PageSize=5 Name=x`.
2. Run with `dotnet run -p:UseRdg=true` and send the same request. The response is `Page=0 PageSize=0 Name=x`.

In the generated `GeneratedRouteBuilderExtensions.g.cs`, the object is created as `new global::DerivedQuery { Name = Name_local }`. The file does not mention `Page` or `PageSize`.

### Exceptions (if any)

None. Both builds report no warning or error.

### .NET Version

SDK 10.0.302, Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 10.0.10, Request Delegate Generator 10.0.10.0

### Anything else?

Workaround: map the endpoint so that the generator cannot resolve the handler, for example through a helper method that takes a `Delegate` parameter and calls `MapGet`. The runtime binder then handles the endpoint.

Issues.Title: Kestrel HTTP/3: `_requestBodyStarted` not reset when a pooled `Http3Stream` is reused
Issues.Body:
`Http3Stream` objects are reused across requests on the same QUIC connection. `Http3Stream.Initialize()` does not reset `_requestBodyStarted`, which is set when a DATA frame is received ([Http3Stream.cs:1002](src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/Http3/Http3Stream.cs)). `Http2Stream.Initialize()` resets its equivalent (`Http2Stream.cs:56`).

After a pooled `Http3Stream` has handled a request with a DATA frame, later body-less requests on that object are misclassified:

- `ReceivedEmptyRequestBody` returns `false`, so `CreateMessageBody()` returns a regular body instead of `MessageBody.ZeroContentLengthClose`.
- `IHttpRequestBodyDetectionFeature.CanHaveBody` is `true` for a request with no body.

### Impact

- Minimal APIs with an optional JSON body (e.g. `Item?`) return 415 because no JSON `Content-Type` is present.
- MVC `[FromBody]` with `EmptyBodyBehavior.Allow` skips the empty-body path and fails the same way.
- Required-body and form endpoints return 415 instead of 400.

The state persists for the life of the pooled stream object, so sequential body-less requests on that connection keep failing. It clears when the stream is evicted from the pool, aborted, or the connection closes.

### Repro

1. Enable HTTP/3 on Kestrel and map `app.MapPost("/x", (Item? item) => Results.Ok(item))`.
2. On one QUIC connection, send a POST with a DATA frame and let it complete.
3. Send a body-less request to `/x` without `Content-Type`.

**Actual:** 415. **Expected:** the body is treated as absent (`CanHaveBody == false`).

### Suggested fix

Reset `_requestBodyStarted = false` in `Http3Stream.Initialize()` and add a test (body request followed by body-less request on a reused stream), e.g. next to `Http3ConnectionTests.StreamPool_*`.

# Harden identity redirect handling in Blazor template

# SignalR: index connections by user in DefaultHubLifetimeManager

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (No issue yet. Opened as a draft so the design can be discussed here; happy to open an issue instead if you'd prefer.)

Send to a user without scanning every connection

## Description

`DefaultHubLifetimeManager.SendUserAsync` and `SendUsersAsync` call `SendToAllConnections` with a filter on `UserIdentifier`. So every `Clients.User(id).SendAsync(...)` enumerates every connection on the server, even though only that user's one or two connections receive the message. Group sends, connection sends and the Redis backplane (one subscription per user) are all indexed already. The default manager's user sends are the only ones that scan.

Measured on shipped .NET 8.0.28 (16-core Windows 11). N connections in one process, connection *i* signed in as `user{i}`, 8 tasks sending for 5 s. Each send reaches exactly one connection.

| connections | `Clients.User` sends/s | `Clients.Client` sends/s | CPU per user send |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 198,713 | 3,720,632 | 49 µs |
| 10,000 | 11,483 | 3,329,994 | 708 µs |
| 50,000 | 1,604 | 2,326,362 | 4.95 ms |

### Change

- `_users` is a second `HubGroupList` keyed by user identifier. It is filled in `OnConnectedAsync` and emptied in `OnDisconnectedAsync`. A user send writes to that user's entry through `SendToGroupConnections`, the same path `SendGroupAsync` uses.
- `HubConnectionHandler` keeps the user identifier fixed after connect ("lifetime managers have no contract for rekeying an existing connection"). The setter is public, though, so:
  - the connection records the id it was indexed under (internal `HubConnectionContext.IndexedUserIdentifier`), and the disconnect removes exactly that entry;
  - sends still compare the live `UserIdentifier`, so a send to the old id skips a connection whose id was changed away from it, as before;
  - a send to the **new** id would not reach such a connection, whereas the scan would. This matches the Redis backplane, which subscribes by the connect-time user id, and relies on the id being fixed at connect as `HubConnectionHandler` states.
- Two cases keep the existing scan:
  - a `null` user id, which matches anonymous connections, and those are not indexed;
  - `SendUsersAsync` with more than 16 ids, following the `SendConnectionsAsync` change in #69189.
- Duplicate ids in `SendUsersAsync` are skipped, so each connection is still written once.

### Results

`SendUsersBenchmark` is added under `src/SignalR/perf/Microbenchmarks`. It uses one connection per user and runs BenchmarkDotNet with the in-process toolchain, on `main` before and after this change.

| connections | `SendUserAsync` before | after | `SendUsersAsync` (10 users) before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 664 ns | 315 ns | 1,214 ns | 2,021 ns |
| 1,000 | 26,330 ns | 333 ns | 49,013 ns | 2,094 ns |
| 10,000 | 816,697 ns | 380 ns | 1,177,521 ns | 2,057 ns |

One regression: a 10-user `SendUsersAsync` on a 10-connection server goes from 1.2 µs to 2.0 µs, and allocation goes from 320 to 896 B. Looking up ten small per-user dictionaries costs more than scanning ten connections. That is the per-group cost `SendGroupsAsync` already pays. If you would rather avoid it, the indexed path could be limited to when the id count is well below the connection count.

### Tests

10 new tests are added to `DefaultHubLifetimeManagerTests`. They check that:
- every connection of a user receives and nobody else does, with ordinal comparison;
- disconnected connections do not receive;
- a user who reconnects after all their connections left receives again;
- a `null` user reaches only connections without a user;
- a connection whose `UserIdentifier` was reassigned is skipped;
- `SendUsersAsync` handles duplicate and missing ids at 16 and 17 targets, as a list and as an array.

The new tests also pass on `main`, so they pin existing behaviour. Leaving out the removal on disconnect makes `SendUserAsyncDoesNotWriteToDisconnectedConnections` fail. The SignalR server suite (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Tests`) has 512 passed and 1 skipped, the same as `main`.

# Add Web Locks API to Components.Platform

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Add navigator.locks as Window.Navigator.Locks with request() and query()

## Description

Ports the [Web Locks API](https://w3c.github.io/web-locks/) to `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Platform`, mapped one-to-one from the Web IDL. API proposal: #70841

**Public API**
- `Window.Navigator.Locks` returns the shared `LockManager` (`NavigatorLockManagerExtensions`).
- `LockManager.RequestAsync(name, callback)` and `RequestAsync(name, LockOptions, callback)`. The callback is a `Func<Lock?, Task>`, and the browser holds the lock until the returned `Task` completes. An exception from the callback releases the lock and is thrown from `RequestAsync` unchanged.
- `LockManager.QueryAsync()` returns a `LockManagerSnapshot` with the held and pending `LockInfo` entries.
- `Lock`, `LockOptions` (`Mode`, `IfAvailable`, `Steal`), and the `LockMode` Web IDL enum struct.
- Every member throws `NotSupportedException` when the page has no `navigator.locks`, such as on an insecure page.

**Deferred:** `LockOptions.signal`. It waits for the package's `AbortSignal` → `CancellationToken` mapping (#70045, or #70328 / #70826). A `CancellationToken` overload can be added later without a breaking change.

**Callbacks from JavaScript to .NET**
`request()` needs the package's first callback from JavaScript to .NET that isn't an event. It reuses the existing event bridge (`JSCallbackFactory`, `JSCallback<T1>`, `createCallback`, `ArgumentShape`) and adds no JavaScript. The new internal `JSCallbackFactory.InvokeWithCallbackAsync` runs an operation that calls a callback at most once:
- It creates the JS function, passes it to the operation, and releases the function and its `DotNetObjectReference` when the operation settles.
- If the callback throws, it rethrows the original .NET exception instead of the `JSException` from the rejected promise. A plain `catch` is used instead of an exception filter, because in WebAssembly the filter clause was never evaluated and the `JSException` reached the caller.

`FeatureContext.CallbackFactory` now exposes the shared factory, which events also use.

**Known limitation (Interactive Server):** the JS promise that waits for the .NET callback does not settle when the circuit's connection drops. In a manual check, the browser still held the lock 60 seconds after going offline, and other tabs keep waiting until a reconnect or a page unload. WebAssembly is not affected. A fix would be internal (the framework or `Platform.ts` settling pending callback promises on disconnect) and is left for a follow-up.

**Tests**
- `LockManagerTest`, 25 tests:
  - acquisition, sharing, missing `navigator.locks`, and disposal
  - the snapshot and options JSON through the real serializer, and every `LockMode` value
  - the lock held until the callback completes, a `null` lock when not granted, and callback exceptions
  - the function released in every path
- `PublicApiTest` covers `LockManager`.
- E2E, in Interactive Server and WebAssembly:
  - `QueryAsync` reads locks held and requested by the page's JavaScript.
  - A lock is held from .NET and checked from JavaScript, then checked again after release and after the callback throws.
  - Each `LockOptions` member is sent, which also covers trimming. The tests pass from the `dotnet publish` output.

API proposal is here: #70841
Related to: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/69876

Issues.Title: Design to generate Blazor page URLs from component types
Issues.Body: ## Summary Add a Blazor routing API that generates an absolute URL from a component's declared routes and named route values. Apps can render that URL in an anchor or pass it to the existing `NavigationManager.NavigateTo` API. ## Motivation and goals In #59356, the author describes maintaining a URL constant for a list page and a URL-building method for a detail page alongside their `@page` directives. The common caller is an app developer who already has the destination type and an identifier, such as an order ID from a list row. The proposed API lets that caller use the page's declaration without repeating its template or manually formatting the identifier. The [feedback on dotnet/aspnetcore#67294](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67294#issuecomment-4749089617) was that `NavigationManager` should not depend on higher-level routing concepts. That PR closed without merge; the feedback does not approve a separate routing service. This proposal keeps URL generation in Blazor routing and leaves navigation with its existing owner. ## In scope - **Proposed first release, subject to the feasibility check below:** literal routes and required named, whole-segment parameters, unconstrained or constrained with `int`. Reuse routing's invariant formatting and path escaping. Bind only supplied values; do not copy ambient values from the current page. - Produce an absolute URI under the current application's base URI, including a non-root base path. Use the same URI for anchor links and programmatic navigation. - Target the same supported route subset in static SSR, Interactive Server (including Blazor Server), and WebAssembly (standalone or interactive in a Blazor Web App). URL generation needs an initialized base URI, not an interactive `Router`. Programmatic navigation retains the host and render-mode behavior of the existing API. - Report missing route declarations, unbindable values, unsupported patterns or policies, and ambiguous aliases explicitly. ## Out of scope - Changing inbound discovery, matching, route precedence, endpoint registration, or component activation. - Enabling general HTTP `LinkGenerator` support for Razor component endpoints or importing server endpoint services into WebAssembly. - Adding a generic navigation wrapper to either the generator or `NavigationManager`. The existing navigation overload already accepts the generated URL. - Optional parameters, defaults, catch-alls, complex segments, and additional route policies (including regex, custom constraints, and transformers) are not promised for the first release. Revisit them only after identifying shared outbound binding and validating host parity. - Inferring query-string keys from component properties or treating unknown route values as query parameters. Use existing query-string helpers to add query values explicitly to the generated URI. - Compile-time validation of route value names and types, verifying app-wide registration or inbound route selection, and adding canonical-route metadata or an alias selector. ## Risks / unknowns - **Shared binding:** Components source-links the routing parser and inbound matcher, but not the outbound binder. Server Razor component endpoints explicitly opt out of link generation. A reusable portion of outbound binding must work without HTTP endpoint dependencies and without changing existing `LinkGenerator` output. If it cannot be shared, reconsider the design rather than introduce a second parser or formatter. - **Host parity and footprint:** Check browser payload size and preservation of route metadata in trimmed/AOT builds. A policy outside the supported subset must fail explicitly even if the current host supports it for inbound routing. ## Examples Assume `Orders` declares `@page "/orders"` and `OrderDetails` declares `@page "/orders/{Id:int}"`. The component type is checked at compile time; route names and values are checked at runtime. `nameof(OrderDetails.Id)` follows a CLR property rename but does not check the `@page` token. Even a successfully generated URI does not prove that the component is registered in the current app or that inbound routing will select it. ```razor @using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Routing @inject ComponentRouteUrlGenerator Routes @inject NavigationManager Navigation @{ var orderUrl = Routes.GetUri(OrderRouteValues).AbsoluteUri; } All orders Order 42 @code { private static readonly IReadOnlyDictionary OrderRouteValues = new Dictionary { [nameof(OrderDetails.Id)] = 42 }; } ``` With the base URI `https://example.com/store/`, the anchor and button use exactly `https://example.com/store/orders/42`. In an app where that route maps to `OrderDetails`, both reach it with `Id == 42`. The anchor works in static SSR; the button requires an interactive render mode. | Declared aliases on one component | Supplied values | Result under `https://example.com/store/` | |---|---|---| | `/orders` and `/orders/{Id:int}` | none | `https://example.com/store/orders` | | `/orders` and `/orders/{Id:int}` | `Id = 42` | `https://example.com/store/orders/42` | | `/orders/{Id:int}` and `/order-history/{Id:int}` | `Id = 42` | `InvalidOperationException`: both aliases bind. Use an explicit URI to select one. | ## Detailed design ### Candidate API An illustrative ref-assembly diff against the current public surface (all additions): ```diff +namespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Routing +{ + public sealed class ComponentRouteUrlGenerator + { + public System.Uri GetUri(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyDictionary? routeValues = null) + where TComponent : Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.IComponent; + } +} ``` `GetUri` is synchronous and returns a non-null, absolute `Uri`. It binds declared templates; it does not do an inbound route lookup or guarantee which component a request will activate. The sealed service belongs in the shared Components assembly, under `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Routing`, not in the server endpoint assembly. It exposes no public constructor or extensibility contract. Named values fit the routing model and avoid positional differences between aliases; `null` means no values, so literal pages need no argument. ### Registration and lifetime Use the existing host registration paths, with no new public registration method. The generator should consume the current scope's initialized `NavigationManager.BaseUri`, not the current page URI. Keep registration idempotent and avoid resolving the generator before the host initializes navigation. | Where the component renders | Proposed registration | Base URI source | |---|---|---| | Static SSR, including prerendering of interactive components | Scoped via `AddRazorComponents` | Current request's `HttpNavigationManager` | | Interactive Server | Scoped via `AddServerSideBlazor`, including the Blazor Web App server registration path | Current circuit's `RemoteNavigationManager` | | Standalone or Interactive WebAssembly | Scoped via `WebAssemblyHostBuilder`; scoped services live for the client app | Client host's `WebAssemblyNavigationManager` | Prerendered Interactive WebAssembly or Auto uses the server request's service during prerendering and the destination runtime's own service after activation. No service state is carried across that transition. Do not add a generator-owned route metadata cache initially. If measurements justify one, clear affected declarations and derived binding state through the existing Components Hot Reload mechanism on supported metadata updates. That invalidation must make the next call observe the updated template without restarting the app. ### Candidate binding rules 1. Read non-inherited route declarations with the same metadata and parser that Blazor routing uses. `RouteData` describes a completed inbound match; it is not the source of templates. 2. Compare names case-insensitively. Rule out templates that do not account for all supplied names or lack a required value. For supported templates, format and escape values using the shared outbound binding logic and evaluate the supported constraint. An `int` constraint checks the formatted value, not the boxed CLR type. Invalid values, such as `"abc"` for `{Id:int}`, do not bind. 3. If two or more supported templates bind, report ambiguity. Otherwise, if the supplied names and required values cannot rule out a template with an unsupported shape or policy, report it as unsupported. Only return a URI when exactly one template binds and no candidate remains unevaluable. Never use reflection order or inbound precedence as a tie-breaker. 4. Resolve the bound path beneath the application base URI without resetting its path. Keep formatting, escaping, and constraint evaluation aligned with the shared routing implementation. ### Failure contract Use documented exceptions for caller and route configuration errors; do not add a result type or `TryGetUri` until there is a concrete scenario for non-throwing probing. The messages should distinguish these cases and identify the component and the relevant names, template, or policy without requiring callers to parse the message for control flow. | Condition | Behavior | |---|---| | Supplied names differ only by case, such as `Id` and `id` | `ArgumentException` for `routeValues`. | | Component declares no route | `InvalidOperationException` explaining that there is no declared route. | | No supported template can bind because required values are missing, extra names are supplied, or values are unformattable or fail a supported constraint | `InvalidOperationException` explaining that no route binds. A null value cannot satisfy a required parameter. | | Two or more supported templates bind | `InvalidOperationException` reporting ambiguity. Callers can use an explicit URI; no alias is chosen. | | Fewer than two supported templates bind, and an otherwise eligible template cannot be evaluated because of an unsupported shape or policy | `NotSupportedException` identifying the template or policy. Do not ignore the policy or return a potentially ambiguous URI. |

Issues.Body:
Backport of #70796 to release/11.0

/cc @oroztocil

# Harden identity redirect handling in Blazor template

Validate return URLs in the Blazor Identity template's redirect manager

## Description

`IdentityRedirectManager.RedirectTo` in the Blazor Web App template (Individual accounts) checks the raw redirect string, and the check can be bypassed. For example, `returnUrl=https://app.example///evil.example` redirects to `https://evil.example/` after sign-in. This change resolves the URI against the app's base URI and only uses it if the result stays within the app. Anything else redirects to the home page.

## Customer Impact

Apps created from the template have an open redirect. A crafted sign-in link can send users to another site after they sign in. Only newly created apps get the fix. Existing apps need to update their copy of `IdentityRedirectManager`.

Issues.Title: Fix Blazor WebAssembly startup options set by JS initializers
Issues.Body:
### Description
Ensure startup options assigned by JavaScript initializers in standalone Blazor WebAssembly take effect.

### Root cause
The framework applies startup options to the runtime builder before invoking JavaScript initializers. Changes made in `beforeStart(options)` were therefore ignored by the runtime builder.

### Fix
Capture the option values before invoking initializers, then reapply any changed `loadBootResource`, `configureRuntime`, `environment`, and `applicationCulture` values afterward.

Existing startup configuration remains unchanged when initializers do not modify these options. No public API changes are introduced.

### Test
Added regression coverage for custom resource loading, environment overrides, application culture, and runtime configuration.

Verified that all four regression tests fail without the fix and pass with it. All 39 selected tests passed, including existing startup-option and localization controls.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54358

Issues.Title: Fix HTTP/3 handshake failure when Kestrel SNI is configured
Issues.Body:
Fixes #70798

## Problem

With Kestrel SNI configuration enabled, HTTP/3 handshakes fail
(`no_application_protocol`) while HTTP/2 over TCP works. Without SNI it works.

## Cause

- `SniOptionsSelector` configures the cached `SslServerAuthenticationOptions`
  with `HttpsConnectionMiddleware.ConfigureAlpn`, which only adds `h2` and
  `http/1.1`.
- `HttpsConfigurationService` returns those options unchanged from the HTTP/3
  `TlsConnectionCallbackOptions.OnConnection`.
- `QuicConnectionListener` only falls back to the listener's protocols (`h3`)
  with `ApplicationProtocols ??= ...`, i.e. when the callback returned `null`.
  With SNI the list is non-null (`[h2, http/1.1]`, or empty for an `Http3`-only
  SNI section), so the connection ends up without `h3`.

Without SNI, `CreateHttp3Options` sets `[h3]` explicitly, which is why it works.

## Fix

In `HttpsConfigurationService`, ensure the options returned by a TLS callback
contain `h3` for QUIC. If they already contain `h3`, or `ApplicationProtocols`
is `null`, they are returned as is. Otherwise they are cloned (the SNI options
are cached and shared with TCP connections) with `ApplicationProtocols = [h3]`.

## Tests

- `HttpsTests` (unit): a callback returning TCP ALPN gets `[h3]` without
  modifying the original instance; a callback without ALPN is unchanged.
- `Http3TlsTests` (QUIC):
  - `TlsHandshakeCallbackOptions_TcpApplicationProtocols_StillNegotiatesHttp3`
    (non-empty TCP list, same error as in the issue).
  - `SniConfiguration_NegotiatesHttp3` (configuration-based `Sni` section).
- Both integration tests fail without the fix and pass with it.

## Notes for review

- The fix adds `h3` for any SNI entry, including one whose `Protocols` doesn't
  include `Http3`. Before, such an entry could not serve HTTP/3 (the handshake
  failed). Honoring the entry's `HttpProtocols` for QUIC would need a change in
  `SniOptionsSelector`. Happy to do that instead if you prefer it at that layer.
- Tested on Windows 11 (MsQuic) with a .NET 12 preview SDK. Not tested on
  Linux/macOS.

Issues.Title: Marshal AbortSignal and CancellationToken across Blazor JS interop
Issues.Body:
- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).

Marshal AbortSignal and CancellationToken across Blazor JS interop

## Description

This implements the API proposal #70826. It supersedes #70328 by @javiercn and keeps his five commits at the start of the branch. The proposal explains the behavior that applications see. No public API changes. This description covers the implementation.

### One rule holds everything together

**"released" always reaches the receiver after every message that carries the id.**

Both directions give each signal or token an id, and both sides keep state per id until the other side sends "released". The messages that carry an id can arrive out of order.

- Interactive Server can reorder inbound messages, because an app can delay them with an inbound activity handler (`CircuitHandler.CreateInboundActivityHandler`).
- The WPF and WinForms WebView hosts send at once on the UI thread, but queue sends from other threads.
- In WebAssembly, a synchronous `[JSInvokable]` result is sent by returning, after anything sent while it was serialized.

So a cancel or an abort may arrive before the message that carries its id, and the receiver must still apply it. And the receiver may forget an id only when nothing that carries the id can still arrive.

### JavaScript signal to .NET token

- The JavaScript call dispatcher (`CallDispatcher` in `Microsoft.JSInterop.ts`) gives each `AbortSignal` one id. In the JSON of the call, it writes `{"__abortSignal": id, "aborted": bool}` in place of the signal. The call is sent at once. There is no setup round trip.
- On the .NET side, the JSON converter (`CancellationTokenJsonConverter.Read`) finds or creates a `CancellationTokenSource` for the id, and gives its token to the method.
- When the signal is aborted, JavaScript sends `__AbortSignalAborted [id]` to .NET as a call that waits for a reply. If it arrives before the call that carries the id, .NET creates the entry already canceled.
- When the browser collects the signal (detected with a JavaScript `FinalizationRegistry`), JavaScript sends `__AbortSignalReleased [id]` to .NET as a one-way message. Before it sends it, JavaScript waits until .NET has answered every call that carried the id and has answered the abort message.
- A signal in a value that a JavaScript function returns to .NET is held the same way, until the .NET method that processes replies from JavaScript (`DotNetDispatcher.EndInvokeJS`) sends `__AbortSignalResultRead [taskId]`. It sends this after processing any successful reply whose JSON contains `"__abortSignal"`, so a value that no JSON converter reads still ends the hold.

### .NET token to JavaScript signal

- .NET gives each token one id from a process-wide counter and writes `{"__dotNetCancellationToken": id, "isCancellationRequested": bool}`. A canceled token and `CancellationToken.None` are written with a `null` id. The counter is process-wide because a WebView page that reloads gets a new runtime but can still receive messages that the old one queued.
- `JSRuntime` finds the entry of a token by the token's hash code, so the same token gets the same id on every call. For each id, a `CancellationTokenLink` (a new internal class) owns the callback registered on the token with `CancellationToken.Register`, and `JSRuntime` refers to the link only through a `WeakReference<T>`. So once the `CancellationTokenSource` that created the token is disposed or collected, the link can be collected too, and `JSRuntime` never keeps the source alive.
- .NET registers the callback on the token after the message is handed to the host, so the callback never runs while .NET serializes a message for JavaScript. When the token is canceled, the callback sends `__CancellationTokenCanceled [id]` to JavaScript as a one-way message.
- The JavaScript call dispatcher keeps the `AbortController` of each id in a JavaScript `Map` until "released", because a browser operation such as `fetch()` does not keep its signal alive. A cancel message for an unknown id creates an `AbortController` that is already aborted. The call to `AbortController.abort()` is deferred with `queueMicrotask`, so in WebAssembly the abort listeners run after `CancellationTokenSource.Cancel()` returns.
- Release. After each message to JavaScript, .NET checks whether links were collected, at most once per garbage collection. For the collected links, it queues `__CancellationTokenReleased [ids]` on the thread pool. A message holds its links until it is sent, so a collected link means that every message with the id is already with the host. Sending from the thread pool keeps the WPF and WinForms hosts from sending "released" ahead of a queued message.
- When `CancellationTokenSource.TryReset()` is called on the source that created a token, the next message with that token gets a new id. This is because the source notifies only the callbacks registered after the reset. .NET detects the reset when `CancellationTokenRegistration.Unregister()` on the old registration returns `false`.
- The `WeakReference<T>` to each link is created with `trackResurrection: true`, so a source that a finalizer cancels still sends its cancel. `JSRuntime.Dispose()` disposes the registration of every link, so a long-lived `CancellationTokenSource` does not keep the runtime alive.

### Messages between the runtimes

The five messages above use reserved names. The receiver checks the name before it looks up a `[JSInvokable]` method (in .NET) or a JavaScript function, and handles the message itself. This is the same way that `__Dispose` works today, the reserved name that the JavaScript `DotNetObject.dispose()` sends to release a `DotNetObjectReference`. Nothing is added to the `DotNet` object in JavaScript, and the host transports (Server, WebAssembly, WebView) do not change.

Apps that never pass a signal or a token pay for one empty JavaScript `Set` per call from JavaScript, one `GC.CollectionCount` check per message from .NET, and one string search in the JSON of each successful reply from JavaScript.

### Behavior differences from #70328

- No public class `JSCancellationTokenReference`, and no `[DynamicDependency]` attribute to keep a `[JSInvokable]` entry point from being trimmed.
- Synchronous calls work. In WebAssembly, JavaScript can pass a signal to `DotNet.invokeMethod` and `DotNetObject.invokeMethod`, and .NET can pass a token to `IJSInProcessRuntime.Invoke`.
- In #70328 a signal that JavaScript code dropped (for example after giving it to `fetch()`) could be collected, and a later cancel was lost.
- One token gives the same `AbortSignal` until it is canceled, or until `CancellationTokenSource.TryReset()` is called on its source. #70328 created a new signal each time the token was serialized.

### Contract

- An `AbortController.abort()` after the call starts may reach .NET after the method has begun running. Only a signal that is aborted before the call is guaranteed to give an already canceled token.
- Disposing a `JSRuntime` does not cancel the tokens made from JavaScript signals. The token means that the JavaScript caller aborted, not that the circuit ended. Work such as a save that is still running when the user closes the tab must not be canceled.

### Known limitations

- On Interactive Server, a message sent while the circuit is disconnected is lost and not sent again after the reconnect, as other interop messages are. This covers abort, cancel, "released", and result read messages, and also a long-polling POST that a proxy rejects. The state for those ids stays until the circuit ends.
- After a Server circuit is disposed, the browser-side `CircuitManager` of that circuit stays referenced until the next circuit starts (`Boot.Server.Common.ts`). Its JavaScript call dispatcher keeps its `AbortController`s and result holds until then or until the page unloads. Fixing this needs a change in `CircuitManager`.
- A canceled, disposed, or collected id stays on both sides until .NET sends its next message to JavaScript after a garbage collection.
- After a WebView reload, a stale result read message from the old page can end a result hold of the same task handle.
- Calls that are pending when a circuit pauses never complete after it resumes, so their ids stay.
- A signal from another realm (an iframe) fails the `instanceof AbortSignal` check and is not recognized. Element references have the same limit with `instanceof Element`.
- The WebView ordering rests on how the WebView hosts dispatch sends to the UI thread, and has no automated test. Native AOT and trimming, multithreaded WebAssembly, and Auto render mode transitions are not validated yet.

### Tests

- `CancellationTokenReferenceTest` (unit, 47 test methods) checks the messages that .NET sends and receives, in arrival orders that the hosts can produce, with garbage collection, finalizers, `CancellationTokenSource.TryReset()`, failed sends, and synchronous calls.
- `AbortSignalArguments.test.ts` and `CancellationTokenArguments.test.ts` (jest, 26 tests) check the JavaScript side, with a fake `FinalizationRegistry` that the tests trigger.
- `InteropCancellationTest` (Selenium, 24 test methods) runs in WebAssembly and Interactive Server. It collects garbage in the browser and in .NET to check that dropped signals still abort and that released ids go away. The Server tests that need reordered messages use a test-only inbound activity handler (`InboundActivityGateHandler`) that holds one message back, so they are deterministic.
- All pass locally. JSInterop unit tests 226/226, Web.JS jest 334/334, and `InteropCancellationTest` plus `InteropTest.CanInvokeInteropMethods` 52/52 (Server and WebAssembly).

The `README.md` of `Microsoft.JSInterop` has a new section that describes the behavior.

Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)

3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "[Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time" (#537)

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

If you were not calling `app.UseAntiforgery()` before you will start using CSRF protection as the defense mechanism from now on.

### Affected APIs

None. This is a behavioral change affecting Blazor SSR form processing and antiforgery-token generation.

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

> Update: The ASP.NET Core 2.3 end of support date was updated from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages (latest patched version only) are currently [supported](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/aspnet#dotnet-core) on .NET Framework, following the support cycle for those .NET Framework versions. After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

## Impact of end of support

After ASP.NET Core 2.3 reaches end of support:

- No new security updates will be issued for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- Continuing to use an unsupported version may expose your applications to security vulnerabilities.
- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- The ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages will be deprecated.

## Upgrade recommendation

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

To help with the upgrade process, we recommend using [GitHub Copilot modernization](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/porting/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview), which provides AI-powered assistance to help you analyze, plan, and execute your migration to a modern .NET version.

Issues.Title: Add automation to create docs tracking issues for breaking changes
Issues.Body:
Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

## Implementation

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

- Triggers on `issues.opened` and `issues.labeled` events with "Breaking change" label
- Creates issue in docs repo with:
  - Title: `[Breaking Change] <original title>`
  - Body: Link to source issue, full context
  - Labels: `breaking-change`, `aspnet/Announcements`
- Posts comment on source issue with link to docs issue

## Duplicate Prevention

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating
- Concurrency control keyed on issue number

## Error Handling

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

## Setup Required

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

## Security

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Deprecating WebHostBuilder,  IWebHost, and WebHost
Issues.Body:
### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

### New behavior

Using `WebHostBuilder` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR004**:
> warning ASPDEPR004: WebHostBuilder is deprecated in favor of HostBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/004.

Using `IWebHost` or `WebHost` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR008**:
> warning ASPDEPR008: WebHost is obsolete. Use HostBuilder or WebApplicationBuilder instead. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/008.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [x] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [ ] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

We recommend the use of `HostBuilder` and `WebApplication` going forward over `WebHostBuilder` because they have all the features of `WebHostBuilder` and will be the focus of future investment.

### Recommended action

See https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host or https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/webapplication for more details on the different hosting models. As well as [HostBuilder replaces WebHostBuilder](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder) and [Introducing WebApplication](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) for migration guides.

Below is an example of converting `WebHostBuilder` to `HostBuilder`:

**Before**
```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

**After**
```csharp
using var host = new HostBuilder()
    .ConfigureWebHost(webHostBuilder =>
    {
        webHostBuilder
            .UseTestServer() // If using TestServer
            .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
            .UseStartup()
            .UseKestrel();
    })
    .Build();
await host.StartAsync();

var testServer = host.GetTestServer();
```

Both Copilot and ChatGpt have given good results so far when asked to convert a WebHostBuilder example to use HostBuilder. Below is an example prompt:
<details>
<summary>Example AI Prompt</summary>

> Can you convert
>
> var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
>     .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
>     .UseStartup()
>     .UseKestrel();
> // Test code might use TestServer:
> var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
>
> to use HostBuilder.

</details>

### Affected APIs

`public class Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.WebHostBuilder`
`public interface Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHost`
`public static class Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebHost`

### Discussion

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/63480

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Exception diagnostics are suppressed when `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns true
Issues.Body:
### Description

The [ASP.NET Core exception handler middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#exception-handler-page), `UseExceptionHandler()`, is responsible for catching and processing unhandled exceptions from ASP.NET Core requests.

In .NET 8, we introduced [`IExceptionHandler`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler). Implementations of `IExceptionHandler` are registered with dependency injection and invoked by the middleware. An implementation can return `true` from `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` to indicate that the exception has been handled. The middleware stops processing the exception once it has been handled.

In .NET 10, we're changing the default behavior so that the middleware no longer records diagnostics for exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

### Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

### Previous behavior

The exception handler middleware recorded diagnostics about exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

The exception diagnostics are:

- Logging `UnhandledException` to `ILogger`.
- Writing the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HandledException` event to `EventSource`.
- Adding the `error.type` tag to the `http.server.request.duration` metric.

### New behavior

If `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `true`, then exception diagnostics are no longer recorded by default.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

ASP.NET Core users have given feedback that the previous behavior was undesirable. Their `IExceptionHandler` implementation reported that the exception was handled, but the error handling middleware still recorded the error in the app's telemetry.

We are changing ASP.NET Core to follow the behavior expected by users by suppressing diagnostics when `IExceptionHandler` handles the exception. We're also adding configuration options to customize exception diagnostics behavior if needed.

### Recommended action

If you want handled exceptions to continue recording telemetry, you can use the new `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` option:

```cs
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = context => false;
});
```

The context passed to the callback includes information about the exception, the request, and whether the exception was handled. Returning `false` from the callback indicates that diagnostics shouldn't be suppressed. This restores the previous behavior.

### References

- Issue: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54554
- PR: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/59074

### Affected APIs

- `UseExceptionHandler()`
- `IExceptionHandler`
